title: Bullion rose
subtitle: Dimensional roses formed by arranging bullion knots around a centre
excerpt: A bullion rose is built by grouping bullion knots into rings around a tight centre bud. Short knots at the core give a closed bud effect, while longer outer knots curve naturally to suggest open petals. The technique draws on the same wrapped-thread principle as the bullion knot, applied in a planned arrangement.
sourceNotes: Bullion knot documented in Dillmont, T. de, Encyclopaedia of Needlework (1886); Caulfeild, S.F.A. & Saward, B.C., The Dictionary of Needlework (1882). Rose arrangement method carried into modern stumpwork and raised embroidery tradition.

content.text: in concentric rings to suggest the furled layers of a rose. The knots are not altered from their usual method; what changes is the number of wraps, the length of each knot, and the direction it curves. More wraps produce a longer, more curved knot, which forms the wider outer petals. A milliner's needle (also called a straw needle) is essential for this technique. Its shaft is the same width from eye to tip, so the thread wraps slide off in one smooth movement rather than catching at a thicker eye.

items.label: Thread
items.value: Stranded cotton (1 or 2 strands for fine work; 2 or 3 for a fuller rose). Silk or perle cotton also work well.

items.label: Fabric
items.value: Closely woven cotton or linen (quilting cotton, calico, or evenweave). The fabric must be stable enough to resist puckering when the knots are pulled firm.

items.label: Needle
items.value: Milliner's (straw) needle, size 3 to 9 depending on thread weight. A uniform shaft is non-negotiable for bullion knots: the wraps must slide off without snagging.

items.label: Hoop
items.value: A small embroidery hoop or ring frame, 10 to 15 cm across. Taut fabric gives a stable base for the knots and prevents puckering.

content.text: Mark the centre of your rose with a small dot in fabric-safe marker. This is where the bud sits. Bring the needle up at (A) and insert it back down at (B), 2 to 3 mm away. Before pulling through, wrap the thread around the needle 3 to 4 times close to the fabric. Hold the wraps down with your thumb and forefinger, then pull the needle carefully through the wraps. Coax the coil down onto the fabric so it lies flat. This short knot forms the bud at the centre.

Work 2 or 3 inner-ring petals around the bud. For each, bring the needle up at a point on one side of the bud (A) and insert it at a point on the other side (B), making the stitch length 4 to 5 mm. Wrap the thread 5 to 7 times around the needle. Pull through slowly while holding the wraps. The knot will curve naturally; guide it so the curve follows the edge of the bud. Position each inner-ring knot so it touches or slightly overlaps the bud.

Add 4 to 6 outer-ring petals. These are longer: stitch length 6 to 8 mm, with 8 to 12 wraps. More wraps than the stitch length needs will force the knot to curve more tightly, which produces the look of an open, cupped petal. Space the outer knots evenly around the inner ring, angling each one so its curve follows the circular shape of the rose.

Control the direction each knot curves by the angle of the needle when you insert it. Tipping the needle slightly inward (toward the centre) helps the knot bend around the rose rather than lying straight. Do not rush the pull-through. A slow, steady pull while holding the wraps lightly produces a neat, even coil.

Secure the thread on the wrong side after each knot by running it under existing stitches before bringing it up for the next knot. This keeps the back tidy and prevents individual knots from pulling loose if the thread is caught.
Optional: add a few short straight stitches or small sepals at the base of the rose in a darker or green thread to suggest leaves and ground the flower on the fabric.

items.symptom: Wraps catch on the needle eye and bunch up
items.cause: A standard embroidery needle has a wider eye than shaft, so the wraps snag as you pull through.
items.fix: Switch to a milliner's (straw) needle. Its shaft is uniform from tip to eye and the wraps slide off cleanly.

items.symptom: Knots lie straight instead of curving into petal shapes
items.cause: The number of wraps matches the stitch length too exactly, leaving no excess thread to force a curve.
items.fix: Add 2 to 4 more wraps than the stitch length seems to need. The extra thread creates the tension that makes the knot bow outward.

items.symptom: The rose looks uneven or lumpy
items.cause: Knots are placed at random angles rather than arranged to follow the circular shape of the flower.
items.fix: Before stitching, lightly sketch the rose in pencil or fade-away marker: a small circle for the bud, a ring for the inner petals, and the outer ring. Use these guides to place each knot so it radiates from the centre.

items.cause: The thread was not secured on the back between knots.
items.fix: After each knot, run the thread under two or three stitches on the reverse before bringing the needle up for the next one. This holds each knot independently.
